blogs.title: Intrinsic or 404(b)? The Eighth Circuit Reaffirms Prior Gun Sightings as Proof of Possession
blogs.description: The panel leans on United States v. Battle to treat witnesses’ prior observations of the same sawed-off rifle as intrinsic—rather than Rule 404(b)—evidence that proves continuous possession in a felon-in-possession case. This post unpacks the Eighth Circuit’s continued reliance on the intrinsic/extrinsic distinction, the evidentiary upside it gives prosecutors in § 922(g) prosecutions, and the countervailing Rule 403 risks. It also situates the ruling amid broader circuit skepticism about the breadth of “intrinsic” evidence and offers defense strategies (e.g., targeted 403 objections and narrowing the temporal window) when prior-sighting testimony threatens to morph into impermissible propensity proof.

blogs.title: Beyond ACCA: How § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) and Unobjected-to PSR Facts Drove a 292-Month Sentence
blogs.description: Cutbank shows how the § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) “in connection with another felony” enhancement can push the offense level above the Armed Career Criminal guideline’s default, with § 4B1.4(b) instructing courts to apply the greater level. The court affirmed based on PSR facts adopted without objection and applied the Eighth Circuit’s presumption of reasonableness for within-Guidelines sentences. This post analyzes the interplay of ACCA and § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B), the permissibility of using uncharged conduct under Application Note 14(C), the preservation pitfalls at sentencing, and how emerging limits on acquitted-conduct use do—and do not—affect cases like this. It also flags the opinion’s curious reference to a three-level serial-number enhancement, where § 2K2.1(b)(4)(B) ordinarily calls for four—likely a harmless typographical slip but a reminder to double-check Guidelines math.

blogs.title: The Perils of ‘Background’ Hearsay: Course-of-Investigation Testimony Survives Crawford—Again
blogs.description: Rejecting a request for a contemporaneous limiting instruction, the court approved officers’ references to D.F.’s statements for context and held any Confrontation Clause concern evaporated once D.F. testified. Citing Bennett and Charboneau, the panel endorsed the practice of deferring limiting instructions to the close of trial. This post examines the Eighth Circuit’s tolerance for “course-of-investigation” testimony, the enduring Crawford tension when juries hear accusatory statements nominally for context, and practical guidance for trial judges and counsel on tailoring questions, instructing juries, and preserving objections to prevent backdoor hearsay from becoming de facto substantive proof.

blogs.title: Impeachment, Authentication, and an Appellate Nudge: Using Police Reports the Right Way
blogs.description: Defense efforts to impeach a witness with statements reflected in a police report ran aground on authentication requirements: under Cumbie, extrinsic impeachment evidence must be authenticated, and Rule 613(b) demands a proper foundation. The panel also noted—none too gently—that the government unnecessarily broadened the issues on appeal. This post distills the opinion’s practice lessons: how to lay the groundwork to use third-party-authored reports for impeachment, when to call report drafters, and how to avoid appellate issue-creep. It also touches on the court’s 403 call allowing a brief reference to a relative’s shooting death and its harmless-error and cumulative-error analyses in a record with strong physical and testimonial proof.
